Introduction

This week, I will analyze the two FluSight models I have shortlisted and take some notes (which will be stored here). I will try to find some real trends (maybe with linear regression or a deeper analysis of that correlation plot) to look at DTW metrics in more detail. I also want to look at how trends happen over HSAs (? possibly because then I could take a look at some outliers) and look at how trends in states actually do different things. Also also, I think I can look at every row (HSA ID) now because the code is more optimized so that’s nice. Looking forward to it!

Using our sample, we can now look at some key statistics.

metrics = setdiff(names(dtw_results), "ID")

summary = reshape(do.call(rbind, lapply(metrics, \(m) data.frame(Metric = m, Var2 = names(summary(dtw_results[[m]])), Freq = as.numeric(summary(dtw_results[[m]])), row.names = NULL))), idvar = "Metric", timevar = "Var2", direction = "wide")
colnames(summary) = c("Metric", "Minimum", "1st Quartile", "Median", "Mean", "3rd Quartile", "Maximum")
rownames(summary) = NULL
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(var_explain), caption = "Dynamic Time Warping Metric (+ Frechet) Descriptions and Significance")
Dynamic Time Warping Metric (+ Frechet) Descriptions and Significance
Metric Description Significance
mean_abs_lag Average absolute time lag between warped points Larger values indicate greater overall timing mismatch between series
signed_lag Average time lag between warped points Positive values imply HSA occurs later than State; negative values imply HSA leads State
lag_sd Standard deviation of time lag along DTW-warped path Larger values indicate more variable or unstable timing misalignment
dtw_mae Mean absolute error along the DTW-warped path (shape comparison) Larger values indicate greater amplitude mismatch after optimal alignment
dtw_rmse Root mean squared error along the DTW-warped path (large differences penalized) Penalizes large local mismatches, more sensitive to extreme deviations
rmse Root mean squared error along the regular path Baseline mismatch ignoring timing differences; comparison benchmark for DTW metrics
amp_ratio Median ratio of amplitudes along the regular path (HSA % of state) Values > 1 indicate HSA generally larger than State; < 1 indicates smaller
dtw_amp_ratio Median ratio of amplitudes along the DTW-warped path (HSA % of state) Values > 1 indicate HSA is larger than State along warping path; < 1 indicates smaller after alignment
lag_amp_corr Correlation between absolute time lag and amplitude warped difference Positive values suggest larger timing shifts coincide with larger amplitude differences while negative values suggest that larger timing shifts coincide with smaller amplitude differences
frechet Discrete Frechet distance (joint deviation in shape and timing) Lower values indicate more similar trajectories; higher values indicate greater overall deviation (leashed dog and owner, the Frechet distance is the smallest leash required)

dtw_results_long = dtw_results %>% pivot_longer(cols = -ID, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")

ggplot(dtw_results_long, aes(x = value)) + geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.8) + facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free", nrow = 2) + 
  theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Density Plots for All DTW Metrics (+ Frechet)", x = "Value", y = "Density")

I think the most promising statistics are signed_lag, rmse - dtw_rmse (smaller is better), amp_ratio, and Frechet distance.

hsa_dtw$ID = as.character(hsa_dtw$ID)

graph_lag = ggplot(hsa_dtw, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, lag_sd), y = lag_sd)) + 
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue") + coord_flip() 

graph_rmse = ggplot(hsa_dtw, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, (rmse-dtw_rmse)), y = rmse-dtw_rmse)) + 
           geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue") + coord_flip()
       
graph_amp = ggplot(hsa_dtw, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, amp_ratio), y = amp_ratio)) + 
          geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue") + coord_flip()

graph_frechet = ggplot(hsa_dtw, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, frechet), y = frechet)) + 
           geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue") + coord_flip()


(graph_lag + graph_rmse) / (graph_amp + graph_frechet)

ggplot(hsa_dtw, aes(x = fct_reorder(ID, lag_sd), y = lag_sd)) + 
  geom_point(fill = "skyblue") + coord_flip()

This is a correlation matrix for the variables present in the DTW metrics and the socioeconomic variables.

cor_matrix = cor(hsa_dtw_refined %>% select(where(is.numeric)))

corrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "lower",
  tl.col = "black",
  addCoef.col = "black",
    order = "hclust",
  number.cex = 0.6,
  diag = FALSE
)

FluSight notes

During the epiENGAGE sessions in the first breakout session on Thursday, I was able to attend a session that focused on analyzing a few models from the FluSight dashboard. In particular, a few models that predicted exceptionally well were CMU-TimeSeries and Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR.

CMU-Time Series

The model is a AR model with specific data that CMU externally sources, I think. I found another link with more (https://zoltardata.com/model/307)

Cornell_JHU-hierarchSIR

The model is a hybrid SIR - Bayesian hierarchical discrepancy model for infectious disease forecasting. After a quick run-through, I couldn’t find much more about the specifics of their model but this is the type of model.
